newsitem.title: UK: Hopes rise of vaccines for humanity's new scourges.
newsitem.headline: Hopes rise of vaccines for humanity's new scourges.

text.p: A vaccine that protected an entire test group of monkeys against the HIV virus offers the freshest hope for a defence against the AIDS epidemic, scientists said on Monday.
But they said it would be years before such a vaccine could be tested on humans.

Advances in genetics have helped researchers map out precise routes for attacking scourges like HIV, tuberculosis and hepatitis and open the door to real protection, a panel of scientists researching possible vaccines against HIV, tuberculosis and hepatitis told a news conference.
"I think there has been a revolution in the past six months," said Thomas Lehner, an immunologist at Guy's Hospital in London who led the study into the monkey vaccine.
He described the vaccine, a genetically-engineered version of the virus which was injected into seven HIV-infected macaques.

The macaques were infected rectally, to simulate the sexual transmission that most commonly spreads AIDS around the world, and then the vaccine was injected in their groins to target lymph glands that cleanse this area of the body.

Lehner said every macaque got some sort of protection against the virus. Four of the seven macaques showed complete immunity, one had "transient" levels of virus and the other two had levels of the virus in their blood drop by 90 percent.
In contrast, 13 of 14 macaques exposed to HIV but not immunised all had high levels of HIV infection.
"We don't know how long the protection lasts," he admitted. The animals were killed and autopsied after six months.
Other researchers said they were a long way from testing such a method on people.
"We don't know enough yet," said Dr Ann Rees of Britain's Jefferis Research Trust Laboratories. She predicted it would be five years before an AIDS vaccine could be tested on humans.
One problem is that HIV does not infect animals naturally and it is, of course, impossible to infect people to test them. But she said Lehner's macaque study offered good hope.
"Expense is a very important factor," she also pointed out. "It would be quite unrealistic and not in our interest to develop a vaccine that was only possible in countries that could afford it."

Lehner, speaking ahead of a presentation at the British Association for the Advancement of Science annual festival, said he was more optimistic about the chances for a human vaccine but did not guess when this might happen.
He said the macaque vaccine was precisely targeted using molecular genetics. He published a report on his findings in the journal Nature Medicine in July.
Scientists can now model the inside and outside of viruses, too tiny to be seen except with an electron microscope. They can plot out exactly how their protein envelopes look.

Lehner's vaccine homed in on gp-120, which he described as a lump on the virus envelope, and p-27, a protein inside the virus. It primed the immune system to recognise and attack anything that contained these two proteins.
Such technology can also work against other diseases.

"With molecular genetics we can take a virus apart," said Douglas Young, a professor of immunology at Imperial College School of Medicine in London, who is working on a tuberculosis vaccine. He estimated that TB now infects a third of the world's population, making a vaccine a top priority.
